titleText.es: Papá, ¿dónde está el abuelo ahora mismo?
titleText.en: Dad, where is Grandpa right now?
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive, and the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute.

regions.labelEs: CUANDO DESHACES UNA CASA DE LEGO Y MEZCLAS LAS PIEZAS EN LA CAJA, ¿A DÓNDE VA LA CASA?

excludedUnits.rationale: LEGO is the printed international toy-brand name, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Cuando introduces a general repeated situation, and deshaces uses the ordinary present form for one familiar listener.
Dónde carries a written accent because it asks for a place directly.

regions.labelEs: NO, ESO SOLO SON PIEZAS. PUEDEN CONVERTIRSE EN NAVES ESPACIALES O TRENES. LA CASA ES UNA ORDENACIÓN PARTICULAR. LA ORDENACIÓN NO PERMANECE CON LAS PIEZAS Y NO SE VA A NINGÚN OTRO LADO. SIMPLEMENTE DESAPARECE.

applications.explanationEn: Son is a form of ser because piezas identifies what those objects are, rather than where they are.
Pueden changes for the plural pieces, while convertirse remains in its unchanged dictionary form as the possible action.

applications.exampleEs: CONVERTIRSE EN NAVES ESPACIALES O TRENES
applications.explanationEn: Convertirse names the change, en introduces the result, and the coordinated nouns name two possible resulting forms.
Espaciales follows naves in the common neutral order for a description.
Espaciales uses plural -es to match plural naves and has the same plural form with masculine and feminine nouns.

applications.exampleEs: LA CASA ES UNA ORDENACIÓN PARTICULAR
applications.explanationEn: Es is a form of ser because the following noun phrase defines the house's identity rather than its location.
Particular follows ordenación in the common neutral order for a description.
Particular is singular to match singular ordenación and has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

applications.exampleEs: SE VA A NINGÚN OTRO LADO
applications.explanationEn: Se and va form irse for the arrangement, while a introduces the destination phrase ningún otro lado.

applications.exampleEs: NO SE VA A NINGÚN OTRO LADO
applications.explanationEn: No remains before the verb because ningún follows it; the two negative words reinforce one negative meaning in Spanish.
Simple has the same masculine and feminine singular form, so adding -mente creates the adverb simplemente.

excludedUnits.rationale: This visibly checked square is a form-control symbol, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Donante names the person, de introduces the donated material, and órganos names that material.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what normally happens whenever another event happens?
cards.answerEn: Use cuando, then an ordinary present-time verb form, and state the usual result.
cards.noteEn: Cuando can introduce a repeated event or a general fact. For that settled, recurring meaning, both actions can use ordinary present forms. This differs from a specific future event, where Spanish normally changes the verb after cuando to a subjunctive form—a form used when that future event is still pending.

example.en: When it rains, I carry an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: you take apart; you undo (one familiar person)
cards.noteEn: Deshaces is the informal singular present form of deshacer. The verb combines des-, which often reverses an action, with hacer, 'to make or do.'

example.en: You undo the knot carefully.

cards.promptEs: casa de LEGO · piezas · ordenación · donante de órganos
cards.answerEn: a joke about whether identity survives when the same material is rearranged
cards.noteEn: The father distinguishes a LEGO house from the plastic pieces that compose it: once its particular arrangement is gone, the house no longer exists as that object. The later organ-donor choice extends the same unsettling question to a person, whose organs may remain even though their arrangement as one living person does not.

cards.answerEn: of; made of or from (introducing a material)
cards.noteEn: After an object or an expression such as ser de or estar hecho de, de introduces the material that composes it.

example.en: The door is made of metal.

cards.noteEn: Dónde carries a written accent when it directly or indirectly asks about a location. In a direct question, Spanish also uses the opening question mark ¿.

example.en: Where is the station?

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.noteEn: Ir can describe how a situation develops. Cómo va can ask how something is going or how it turns out.

example.en: We'll see how the project goes.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.answerEn: they can; they are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.noteEn: Convertirse is the verb's unchanged dictionary form with se attached. A changing form such as se convierte matches the person or thing that changes; en normally introduces the result.

example.es: La oruga puede convertirse en mariposa.
example.en: The caterpillar can turn into a butterfly.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something becomes or turns into something else?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of convertirse, then en, then name the result.
cards.noteEn: Convertirse is used with a matching short word such as me, te, se, or nos. Change convertir to match the person, thing, and time, but keep en before the resulting identity or form: se convierte en, se convirtió en, or se está convirtiendo en.

example.es: La oruga se convierte en mariposa.
example.en: The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

cards.answerEn: into; introduces the result after convertirse
cards.noteEn: After convertirse, en links the changing person or thing to what it becomes. Keep en even though English may simply use become before a noun.

example.es: El agua se convierte en hielo.
example.en: Water turns into ice.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; it forms irse, 'to leave' or 'to go away'
cards.noteEn: Ir means 'to go.' With a matching short word such as me, te, se, or nos, irse focuses on departure: se va means that someone or something leaves or goes away.

example.es: El último autobús se va a las once.
example.en: The last bus leaves at eleven.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone leaves for or goes off to a destination?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of irse, then a and the destination: me voy a…, se va a…, or nos vamos a….
cards.noteEn: The short word before ir changes with the person: me, te, se, nos, os, or se. Plain ir focuses on going somewhere; irse often highlights leaving the current place. The destination may include an article, as in a la playa or a las islas.

example.en: We are leaving for the beach.

cards.answerEn: it leaves; it goes away (with se)
cards.noteEn: Va is the present form of ir used with one other person or thing. In se va, the added se makes irse and shifts the focus from movement toward somewhere to departure from the current place or state.

example.es: El dolor se va poco a poco.
example.en: The pain goes away little by little.

cards.answerEn: no; not any (before a masculine singular noun)
cards.noteEn: Ningún is used directly before a masculine singular noun. When it comes after the verb, Spanish normally also keeps no before the verb: no tengo ningún problema.

example.en: We did not see any error.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

example.en: Lucía answers clearly.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to an organ donor?
cards.noteEn: Donante names the donor, and de introduces what is donated. Change the noun after de for other kinds of donation, such as donante de sangre.

example.es: Ana decidió ser donante de órganos.
example.en: Ana decided to be an organ donor.

cards.answerEn: of; links a donor to what is donated
cards.noteEn: After donante, de introduces the thing that the person donates: donante de sangre, donante de órganos, or donante de médula.

example.en: They are looking for a blood donor.
